q: What is the maximum gap allowed between two sessions of Parliament?
explain: The Constitution requires that no more than 6 months should elapse between the last sitting of one session and the first sitting of the next session.

q: 'Double Jeopardy' protection in India is guaranteed under:
explain: Article 20(2) protects against double jeopardy — no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once. This is a fundamental right available to all persons.

q: The National Commission for Scheduled Castes draws its constitutional position primarily from:
explain: Article 338 provides for the National Commission for Scheduled Castes.

explain: Correct statements: 1, 2, 3. Incorrect: none. This follows the standard UPSC three-statement option codes.

q: President's Rule (State Emergency) is imposed under:
explain: Article 356 (President's Rule/State Emergency): The President can take over state government if state constitutional machinery fails. Proclaimed on Governor's report (or other information). Parliament must approve every 6 months. Maximum: 3 years.

q: 'Public Interest Litigation' (PIL) was developed by:
explain: PIL was developed by the Supreme Court of India in the 1980s, especially through Justices V.R. Krishna Iyer and P.N. Bhagwati, allowing any citizen to approach courts for public interest.

explain: Correct statements: 1, 2. Incorrect: 3. This follows the standard UPSC three-statement option codes.

q: The Delimitation Commission is established by:
explain: Delimitation Commission is established by an Act of Parliament (Delimitation Act). It determines boundaries of constituencies for Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies.

q: The Pocket Veto (keeping a bill indefinitely) can be exercised by:
opts: The President (for bills with no assent deadline)
explain: For ordinary bills (not Money Bills or Constitutional Amendments), there is no time limit for Presidential assent — the President can keep it indefinitely (pocket veto), as was done by Zail Singh in 1986.

q: Which article guarantees freedom of speech and expression in India?
explain: Article 19(1)(a) guarantees all citizens the right to freedom of speech and expression.

q: A State Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha) member must be at least:
explain: To be a member of a State Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha), a person must be at least 25 years old (Article 173). To vote, the minimum age is 18 years (reduced from 21 by the 61st Amendment, 1988).

1. Attorney General is under Art 76.
2. UPSC is under Art 315.
3. UPSC is concerned with All-India and Central Services recruitment advice.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Correct statements: 1, 2, 3. Incorrect: none. This follows the standard UPSC three-statement option codes.

q: The 'Question Hour' in Parliament is:
opts: The first hour of every parliamentary sitting
The last hour of every sitting
A special session for questions only
explain: Question Hour is the first hour of a parliamentary sitting (11 AM to 12 Noon in Lok Sabha). Starred questions get oral answers; unstarred questions get written answers.

q: Article 1 of the Indian Constitution describes India as:
explain: Article 1 describes India as a 'Union of States' — not a federation. This term was deliberately chosen to indicate that States have no right to secede from the Union (unlike a federation or confederation).

q: Which article deals with the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in disputes between the Centre and States?
explain: Article 131 confers original jurisdiction on the Supreme Court in disputes between the Government of India and one or more States, or between two or more States.

q: The minimum age to become Governor is:
explain: To become a Governor (Article 157): Must be a citizen of India and must have completed 35 years of age. Must not be a member of Parliament or State Legislature.

q: 'Gram Sabha' is a body consisting of:
opts: All registered voters in a village
explain: Gram Sabha is a body consisting of all persons registered in the electoral rolls of the village — the primary democratic unit at grassroots level under the 73rd Amendment.

q: The Sarkaria Commission (1983) was set up to examine:
explain: Sarkaria Commission (1983-87) was set up to examine and review Centre-State relations. It submitted its report in 1988 with 247 recommendations to strengthen cooperative federalism.

q: The Preamble to the Constitution was amended by:
explain: The Preamble has been amended only once — by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act 1976 — which added 'Socialist', 'Secular', and 'Integrity'.

q: The Goods and Services Tax (GST) was introduced by the:
explain: The 101st Constitutional Amendment (2016) introduced GST — inserting Art 246A (concurrent power to levy GST), Art 269A (IGST), Art 279A (GST Council), and amending Schedule 6/7.

q: What are the three types of Government in India?
explain: India has three tiers of government: Central Government, State Government, and Local Self-Government (Panchayats and Municipalities).

q: Which is the correct order of precedence: who comes after the Vice President?
explain: India's official order of precedence: 1. President, 2. Vice President, 3. Prime Minister, 4. Governors (in their states), 5. Former Presidents, 6. Deputy PM, 7. Chief Justice of India / Speaker of Lok Sabha (equal).

q: Which writ is used to produce a detained person before a court?
explain: Habeas Corpus (meaning 'You may have the body') is issued to free a person from illegal detention.

1. Federation with strong Centre — A. Canada
2. Directive Principles — B. Ireland
3. Concurrent List — C. Australia
4. Fundamental Rights — D. USA
Select the correct match:
explain: Canada (strong centre), Ireland (DPSP), Australia (Concurrent List), USA (Fundamental Rights) is the standard mapping.

q: The 42nd Amendment (1976) is called the 'mini-Constitution' because:
opts: Made sweeping changes (Preamble, Fundamental Duties, curtailed judiciary)
It was the 42nd attempt to amend
explain: 42nd Amendment (Indira Gandhi during Emergency, 1976) was the most comprehensive amendment: added 'Socialist' and 'Secular' to Preamble, added 10 Fundamental Duties, gave primacy to DPSPs over Fundamental Rights, curtailed SC/HC powers, extended Lok Sabha/state assembly terms to 6 years.

q: The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act (1992) related to:
opts: Panchayati Raj institutions — gave constitutional status to 3-tier system
Financial relations between states and centre
explain: 73rd Amendment (1992) added Part IX (Articles 243-243O) and 11th Schedule to the Constitution, giving constitutional status to Panchayati Raj. Mandated 3-tier system (Village, Intermediate, District Panchayats), elections, reservation for SC/ST/women (33%), 5-year term.

q: Which Fundamental Right was described as the 'heart and soul of the Constitution' by Ambedkar?
explain: Dr. Ambedkar called Article 32 (Right to Constitutional Remedies) the 'heart and soul of the Constitution' as it gives the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.

q: The presiding officer of a Joint Sitting of Parliament is:
explain: Joint sittings (Art 108) are presided over by the Speaker of Lok Sabha, or in his absence, the Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha, or if he is also absent, the Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha.

q: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992) established:
explain: Indra Sawhney case (Mandal Commission case, 1992): SC upheld OBC reservation but: (a) 50% ceiling on reservations, (b) Excluded creamy layer from OBC reservation, (c) No reservation in promotions.

q:
Assertion (A): Single citizenship is a feature of the Indian Constitution.
Reason (R): Dual citizenship is expressly provided under Article 5 for all persons.
Select the correct answer using the codes below.
opts: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion

Assertion is true but Reason is false
Assertion is false but Reason is true
explain: A is true; R is false — India has single citizenship; Article 5 deals with citizenship at commencement, not dual citizenship.

q: The Finance Commission is constituted under:
explain: Article 280: Finance Commission is constituted by the President every 5 years to recommend distribution of tax revenues between Centre and States and grants-in-aid to states.

q: The concept of 'Equality before law' under Article 14 is borrowed from:
opts: British Constitution (Rule of Law by Dicey)
explain: Article 14's first expression — 'Equality before law' — is borrowed from the British concept of Rule of Law formulated by A.V. Dicey. The second expression — 'Equal protection of laws' — is borrowed from the 14th Amendment of the US Constitution.

q: The Gram Sabha consists of:
opts: All persons registered as voters in the Panchayat area
All adult residents (whether registered voters or not)
explain: The Gram Sabha (Art 243A) consists of all persons registered in the electoral rolls of a village — i.e., all adult voters of that village. It is the foundation of democratic decentralization and can exercise powers as the State Legislature decides.

q: Under Article 239AA, the NCT of Delhi's legislature cannot make laws on:
explain: Art 239AA (inserted by 69th Amendment, 1991) gives Delhi's legislature power on all matters EXCEPT three: Police, Public Order, and Land. These remain with the Central Government. This was upheld by the Supreme Court.

q: Which fundamental right is called the 'Heart and Soul' of the Constitution?
explain: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called Article 32 (Right to Constitutional Remedies) the 'Heart and Soul' of the Constitution.

q:
With reference to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
1. NITI Aayog is a constitutional body.
2. Advocate General advises State Government.
3. National Commission for Backward Classes has constitutional status under Art 338B.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Correct statements: 2, 3. Incorrect: 1. This follows the standard UPSC three-statement option codes.

q: Which article provides that the laws made under Article 249 (national interest) by Parliament cease to have effect after the Rajya Sabha resolution expires?
explain: Article 249(3) provides that a law made by Parliament under Article 249 shall cease to have effect on the expiration of the period (or its extension) specified in the Rajya Sabha resolution.

q: The Parliamentary form of government in India is borrowed from:
explain: Parliamentary system (Cabinet government, Prime Minister's role, collective responsibility) is borrowed from the British (Westminster) model. Also known as Westminster Model.

q: The Right to Property was removed as a Fundamental Right by:
explain: 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) removed Right to Property from Fundamental Rights (Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31). It became a legal right under Article 300A.

q: Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of:
opts: Religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth
explain: Article 15 prohibits discrimination by the State on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, OR place of birth. However, special provisions for women, children, SCs, STs, OBCs are allowed.

q: The 91st Constitutional Amendment (2003) limits the size of the Council of Ministers to:
opts: 15% of the total strength of the Lower House
explain: The 91st Amendment (2003) inserted Art 75(1A) limiting the Council of Ministers to not more than 15% of the total membership of Lok Sabha. Same limit applies to state Cabinets (Art 164(1A)).

q: The Prime Minister is appointed by:
explain: The President appoints the Prime Minister (Article 75). Conventionally, the President appoints the leader of the party/coalition that commands majority in the Lok Sabha. The PM is the head of the Council of Ministers and real executive head.

q: In a democracy, the ultimate power rests with:
explain: In a democracy, ultimate sovereignty rests with the people, who exercise power through their elected representatives.

q: Article 21 guarantees:
opts: Protection of life and personal liberty
explain: Article 21 is one of the most fundamental rights. Through judicial interpretation, it now covers: right to privacy, right to livelihood, right to health, right to clean environment, right to speedy trial, right to dignity, etc. Article 21A guarantees free education for children 6-14 years.

q: The Governor of a state is appointed by:
explain: The Governor is appointed by the President of India (Article 155). The Governor is the constitutional head of the state (like President at national level) and acts as the agent/representative of the Centre in the state.

q: Article 371 deals with:
opts: Special provisions for certain states (like NE states)
explain: Articles 371-371J provide special provisions for certain states: 371A (Nagaland), 371B (Assam), 371C (Manipur), 371D-F (Andhra Pradesh/Telangana), 371G (Mizoram), 371H (Arunachal), 371I (Goa), 371J (Karnataka).

q: Who administers the oath of office to the Vice President of India?
explain: The President administers the oath of office to the Vice President (Art 69). Whereas, the Chief Justice of India administers the oath to the President.

q: The 12th Schedule of the Constitution relates to:
explain: The 12th Schedule (added by 74th Amendment, 1992) contains 18 functions of Municipalities/Urban Local Bodies, like urban planning, regulation of land use, public health, etc.

q: India follows which type of citizenship?
opts: Single citizenship (no dual citizenship for states)
explain: India provides for single citizenship — every citizen is a citizen of India only (unlike USA where citizens have both national and state citizenship). This promotes national unity.

q: The 'Doctrine of Pleasure' in the Indian Constitution is modified in the case of:
opts: Judges of High Courts and Supreme Court
explain: Article 310 provides that government servants hold office 'at the pleasure of the President.' However, this is modified for judges of Supreme Court and High Courts, CAG, UPSC members — they can only be removed through impeachment-like processes.

q: The 15th Finance Commission's recommendations cover the period:
explain: The 15th Finance Commission (Chairman: N.K. Singh) submitted its report covering 2021-2026. It recommended 41% devolution of taxes to States (same as 14th FC's 42%, reduced by 1% due to J&K reorganization).

q: Article 13 of the Constitution deals with:
opts: Voidness of laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights
explain: Article 13: Any law that takes away or abridges Fundamental Rights is void to the extent of inconsistency. It also prohibits the State from making such laws — foundation of judicial review.

q: Collective responsibility of Council of Ministers means:
opts: All ministers are jointly responsible to Lok Sabha
Cabinet is responsible to Rajya Sabha
explain: Article 75: Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to Lok Sabha — all ministers stand or fall together. A vote of no-confidence against any minister means the entire government falls.

q: The Constitution of India originally had:
explain: The original Constitution (1950) had 395 articles, 22 parts, and 8 schedules. After amendments, it now has 448 articles, 25 parts, and 12 schedules. It is the world's lengthiest written constitution.

q: Reservation of seats for women in Panchayats is mandated by:
explain: Article 243D mandates reservation of not less than one-third of seats for women in Panchayats at all levels. Many States (including Tamil Nadu) have increased this to 50% by State law.

q: How many sessions did the Constituent Assembly hold before adopting the Constitution?
explain: The Constituent Assembly held 11 sessions over 2 years, 11 months and 18 days (9 December 1946 – 26 November 1949) before adopting the Constitution.

q: The Constitution describes India as:
explain: Article 1 describes India as a 'Union of States' — not federation. This implies the union is indestructible and states cannot secede. India is not a true federation.

q: Which is the highest court in India?
explain: The Supreme Court of India is the apex court and the final interpreter of the Constitution.

3. Advocate General advises State Government.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Correct statements: 1, 2, 3. Incorrect: none. This follows the standard UPSC three-statement option codes.

q: The 9th Schedule was added by which Constitutional Amendment?
explain: 9th Schedule was added by the 1st Constitutional Amendment (1951) to protect certain land reform laws from judicial review. Laws in 9th Schedule are immune from fundamental rights challenge.

q: When can the Governor reserve a bill for the President's consideration?
opts: When the bill endangers High Court's position or is against Constitution
explain: Governor can reserve a bill for Presidential consideration if it: endangers the position of the High Court, is repugnant to the Constitution, or against the policy of the Union government.

q: Which article empowers the Parliament to create new States or alter the boundaries of existing States?
explain: Article 3 empowers Parliament to form new States by separation, union, or merger of existing States, or by altering boundaries, names, or areas.

q: Article 32 is called the 'Heart and Soul of the Constitution' by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar because:
opts: Right to constitutional remedies (move SC directly)
explain: Article 32 (Right to Constitutional Remedies) allows any citizen to move the Supreme Court directly if their Fundamental Rights are violated. The SC can issue writs (Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, Certiorari). Ambedkar called it the 'very soul of the Constitution'.

q: Which Article deals with the impeachment of the President?
explain: Article 61 deals with impeachment of the President. It can be initiated in either House of Parliament for 'violation of the Constitution'. It requires a 2/3rd majority in both Houses separately.

q: Which article provides for the establishment of the Supreme Court?
explain: Article 124 of the Constitution establishes the Supreme Court of India.

q: Fundamental Duties are contained in:
explain: Fundamental Duties are in Article 51A (Part IVA), added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) based on Swaran Singh Committee recommendations. 11th duty added by 86th Amendment (2002).

explain: The Preamble begins: 'We, the People of India, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic and to secure to all its citizens JUSTICE, LIBERTY, EQUALITY, and FRATERNITY...'

q: The 'Golden Triangle' of the Indian Constitution comprises:
explain: The 'Golden Triangle' or 'Trinity' of the Constitution comprises Articles 14 (Equality), 19 (Freedoms), and 21 (Life and Personal Liberty). These are considered the most important Fundamental Rights, often read together.

q: Which schedule of the Constitution lists the powers and functions of Gram Panchayats?
explain: The 11th Schedule (added by 73rd Amendment, 1992) contains 29 subjects/functions of Gram Panchayats, like agriculture, rural housing, drinking water, education, etc.

q: The DPSP that requires the state to minimize inequalities in income and status is:
explain: Article 38 directs the State to secure a social order for promotion of welfare and to minimize inequalities in income, status, facilities, and opportunities. Article 39 lists specific economic principles (equal pay, no concentration of wealth, etc.).

explain: Correct statements: 2, 3. Incorrect: 1. This follows the standard UPSC three-statement option codes.

q: The office of the District Collector/Collector in India was introduced by:
opts: British East India Company (Lord Cornwallis system)
explain: The office of the Collector was introduced by the British East India Company — primarily by Lord Cornwallis through the Permanent Settlement (1793) system in Bengal. The Collector collects revenue and administers the district.

q: Which DPSP relates to 'Equal pay for equal work for men and women'?
explain: Article 39(d) DPSP directs equal pay for equal work for both men and women — aimed at eliminating gender-based wage discrimination.

q: The first Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu was:
explain: O.P. Ramaswamy Reddiyar was the first Chief Minister of Madras State (1947-1949) after independence. Chakravarti Rajagopalachari became the first CM under the new Constitution in 1952.

q: Who was the Chairman of the Constituent Assembly that drafted the Indian Constitution?
explain: Dr. Rajendra Prasad was the President (Chairman) of the Constituent Assembly. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee.

q: Which article enables the High Courts to issue writs?
explain: Article 226 empowers every High Court to issue writs including Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Certiorari, Prohibition, and Quo Warranto for enforcement of Fundamental Rights and for any other purpose.

q: Which article gives the Supreme Court power to transfer cases from one High Court to another?
explain: Article 139A (added by 46th Amendment) empowers the Supreme Court to transfer cases involving the same or substantially similar questions of law from one High Court to another or to itself.

q: The Governor's address to the State Legislature at the commencement of session corresponds to:
opts: President's address to Parliament (first session of the year)
explain: Just as the President addresses both Houses of Parliament at the commencement of the first session after each election and the first session of each year (Art 87), the Governor addresses the State Legislature (Art 176).

q: The Constitution of India borrowed the idea of Directive Principles from:
explain: Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV, Articles 36-51) were borrowed from the Irish Constitution (1937). The concept was inspired by the Spanish Constitution of 1931.

q: In India, which of the following review the independent regulators in sectors like telecommunications, insurance, electricity etc. ? 1. Ad Hoc Committees set up by the Parliament. 2. Parliamentary Department Related Standing Committees 3. Finance Commission 4. Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission 5. NITI Aayog Select the correct answer using the code given below.
explain: Official UPSC key marks option A as correct for Prelims GS1 2019 Q69. Correct choice: 1 and 2. Ingested from local PYQ corpus with official answer key.

q: Which writ is known as 'Bulwark of personal liberty'?
explain: Habeas Corpus (Latin: 'to have the body') is called the great writ/bulwark of personal liberty. It directs the detaining authority to produce the detained person before court and justify detention.

q: The Preamble of the Indian Constitution begins with which words?
explain: The Preamble begins with 'WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA', emphasizing popular sovereignty.

q: Which symbol appears on the national emblem of India?
opts: Ashoka's Lion Capital with the motto 'Satyameva Jayate'
explain: India's national emblem is adapted from the Lion Capital of Ashoka at Sarnath. It shows four lions and the motto 'Satyameva Jayate' (Truth Alone Triumphs).

q: Which writ commands a public authority to perform a public or statutory duty?
explain: Mandamus (Latin: 'we command') is issued by a superior court to an inferior court, tribunal, or public authority to compel them to perform a ministerial/statutory duty that they have failed to perform.

q: The Preamble declares India as a:
explain: Preamble declares India as a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic (SSSDR). Sovereign=independent; Socialist=social justice; Secular=no state religion; Democratic=elected government; Republic=no hereditary head.

q: Financial Emergency (Art 360) has been invoked in India:
explain: Financial Emergency (Art 360) has never been proclaimed in India. It can be proclaimed when the financial stability or credit of India or any State is threatened.

q: Which article gives the President the power to grant pardon?
explain: Article 72 empowers the President to grant pardon, reprieve, respite, or remission of punishment to persons convicted of offences.

q: Article 19 guarantees freedom to all CITIZENS. Which of these is NOT in Article 19?
opts: Freedom to reside and settle anywhere in India
Right to life and personal liberty
explain: Article 19 gives citizens 6 freedoms: speech/expression, peaceful assembly (without arms), forming associations/unions, free movement, residence/settlement, and practising any profession/occupation. Article 21 (Right to Life and Personal Liberty) is separate.

q: The first Speaker of Lok Sabha was:
explain: Ganesh Vasudev Mavalankar (G.V. Mavalankar) was the first Speaker of Lok Sabha (1952-1956). He is called the 'Father of the Lok Sabha'.

q: The 'Right to be forgotten' relates to:
explain: 'Right to be forgotten' (right to erasure of personal data from internet) flows from Right to Privacy under Article 21, as elaborated in the Puttaswamy judgment (2017).

q: Which constitutional provision disqualifies a person from being a member of Parliament on grounds of holding an office of profit?
explain: Article 102(1)(a) disqualifies a person from being or remaining a member of either House of Parliament if they hold any 'office of profit' under the Government of India or any State government.

q: Article 44 of the Constitution directs the State to secure:
explain: Article 44 directs the State to endeavor to secure a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) for citizens throughout India. This remains one of the most politically sensitive DPSPs yet to be implemented.

q: 'Rajya Sabha' literally means:
explain: 'Rajya Sabha' means 'Council of States' in Hindi. 'Lok Sabha' means 'House of the People'. Rajya Sabha represents the states/UTs of India in Parliament.

q: In the context of Indian federalism, which principle ensures that Centre-State relations involve co-operation rather than subordination?
explain: Co-operative federalism refers to the idea that different levels of government should share power and work together co-operatively, rather than acting in competing interests. India has increasingly moved toward this model.

q: The Rajya Sabha cannot be dissolved because:
explain: Rajya Sabha is a permanent body — it cannot be dissolved. One-third of its members retire every two years. Its members are elected for 6-year terms by elected members of State Legislative Assemblies.

q: The Speaker of Lok Sabha vacates office:
opts: When new Lok Sabha meets for the first time
explain: The Speaker vacates office not when Lok Sabha is dissolved, but 'immediately before the first sitting of the new Lok Sabha' (Article 94). The Speaker thus continues for the first sitting of the new House.

q: The 11th Schedule of the Constitution relates to:
explain: 11th Schedule (added by 73rd Amendment, 1992) contains 29 subjects/functions to be assigned to Panchayats — including agriculture, land improvement, rural roads, health, education, etc.

q: Under Article 352, National Emergency can be proclaimed on grounds of:
opts: War, External Aggression, or Armed Rebellion
explain: National Emergency (Article 352) can be proclaimed on grounds of: (i) War, (ii) External Aggression, or (iii) Armed Rebellion (formerly 'internal disturbance', changed by 44th Amendment).

q: Which Finance Commission is constituted to recommend devolution of taxes between Centre and States under Article 280?
explain: Article 280 provides for the constitution of a Finance Commission every 5 years (or earlier if needed) to recommend the distribution of net proceeds of taxes between the Centre and States.

q:
With reference to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
1. Attorney General is under Art 76.
2. Advocate General is under Art 165.
3. Attorney General has right of audience in all Indian courts.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Correct statements: 1, 2, 3. Incorrect: none. This follows the standard UPSC three-statement option codes.

q: The Concurrent List contains subjects on which:
opts: Both Centre and States can legislate
explain: The Concurrent List (52 items) contains subjects on which both the Parliament and State Legislatures can make laws. In case of conflict, Central law prevails.

q: The Comptroller and Auditor General's role was described as 'the most important officer under the Constitution' by:
explain: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described the CAG as the most important officer under the Constitution of India because the CAG ensures financial accountability and that public money is spent as Parliament intended.

q: Fifth Schedule of the Constitution deals with:
opts: Administration of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes
explain: 5th Schedule: Administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in states (most states). 6th Schedule: Administration of Tribal Areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram.

q: Under Article 3, a new State can be formed by:
explain: Article 3 empowers Parliament to form new States and alter borders by a simple majority (ordinary legislation). The President must refer the Bill to the concerned State Legislature for its views (non-binding).

q: NITI Aayog replaced which body in 2015?
explain: NITI (National Institution for Transforming India) Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015. Unlike Planning Commission, NITI Aayog is a policy think-tank and does not allocate funds directly to States.

q:
With reference to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
1. Attorney General is under Art 76.
2. Advocate General is under Art 165.
3. NHRC is a constitutional body under Art 338B.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Correct statements: 1, 2. Incorrect: 3. This follows the standard UPSC three-statement option codes.

q:
With reference to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
1. NITI Aayog is a constitutional body.
2. UPSC is under Art 315.
3. Attorney General has right of audience in all Indian courts.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Correct statements: 2, 3. Incorrect: 1. This follows the standard UPSC three-statement option codes.

q: The concept of 'due process of law' in India was elaborated in:
opts: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
explain: Maneka Gandhi case (1978): SC interpreted Article 21 broadly — procedure for depriving life/liberty must be fair, just, and reasonable (not mere 'procedure established by law' as literally stated).

q: The concept of 'Judicial Review' in India is:
opts: Limited — courts can review laws for constitutional validity but not policy
explain: India has a limited form of judicial review — courts can strike down laws violating the Constitution (unlike USA's stronger judicial review). The Basic Structure doctrine further limits Parliament's amendment power.

q: 'Privilege Motion' in Parliament is moved against:
opts: Ministers/members for breach of parliamentary privilege
explain: Privilege Motion is moved when a member believes that a minister or another member has committed a breach of parliamentary privilege (e.g., misleading the House, contempt of Parliament).

q:
With reference to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
1. UPSC is under Art 315.
2. NHRC is a constitutional body under Art 338B.
3. NCST is under Art 338A.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Correct statements: 1, 3. Incorrect: 2. Answer follows the standard UPSC 3-statement code set.

q: The Constitution of India was drafted by the Constituent Assembly in how many days?
explain: The Constituent Assembly took 2 years, 11 months, and 18 days (December 9, 1946 to November 26, 1949) to draft the Constitution, holding 11 sessions with 165 sitting days.

q: Fundamental Duties were added to the Constitution by the:
explain: The 42nd Amendment Act (1976) added Fundamental Duties (Part IVA, Article 51A) with 10 duties based on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee. The 86th Amendment (2002) added the 11th duty — to provide opportunities for education to children aged 6-14.

q: Which Article enables Parliament to form new All India Services?
explain: Article 312 empowers Rajya Sabha (by 2/3rd resolution) to declare creation of new All India Services in national interest. Under this, IAS, IPS and Indian Forest Service (IFS) were created. Parliament then makes law.

q: The 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) changed the term 'Internal Disturbance' in Article 352 to:
explain: 44th Amendment (1978) changed 'internal disturbance' to 'armed rebellion' in Article 352, making it harder to impose National Emergency on minor internal disturbances.

q: A Supreme Court judge can be removed by:
opts: Address by both Houses of Parliament followed by Presidential order
explain: SC judge can be removed only on the grounds of proven misbehavior or incapacity by an address passed by special majority in both Houses of Parliament and Presidential order (Article 124).

q: The President of India can be impeached for:
explain: The President can be impeached only for violation of the Constitution (Article 61). The process starts in either House (special majority of 2/3rd) and is ratified by the other House.

q:
With reference to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
1. Attorney General is under Art 76.
2. Finance Commission is under Art 280.
3. NHRC is a constitutional body under Art 338B.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Correct statements: 1, 2. Incorrect: 3. This follows the standard UPSC three-statement option codes.

q: The Finance Commission of India is constituted by:
explain: The Finance Commission (Article 280) is constituted by the President every 5 years. It recommends: how central taxes are shared with states, grants-in-aid to states, and any other matter referred. The 15th Finance Commission (2021-26) recommended 41% tax devolution to states.

q: Which article gives Parliament the power to create new states?
explain: Article 3 empowers Parliament to form new states, increase/decrease areas, alter boundaries or change names of existing states. Such bills require Presidential recommendation.

q: A 'No Confidence Motion' can be moved against:
opts: The Council of Ministers (the Cabinet) in the Lok Sabha
explain: A No Confidence Motion (or Motion of No Confidence) is moved in the Lok Sabha against the Council of Ministers. If passed, the Prime Minister and Cabinet must resign. Requires support of at least 50 Lok Sabha members to be admitted.

q:
With reference to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
1. Attorney General is under Art 76.
2. NITI Aayog is a constitutional body.
3. Finance Commission is under Art 280.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Correct statements: 1, 3. Incorrect: 2. This follows the standard UPSC three-statement option codes.

q: Under Article 110, a Bill is deemed to be a Money Bill if it deals with:
opts: Imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of any tax
Appropriation of money from Consolidated Fund
explain: Article 110 defines a Money Bill. It deals with: taxation, borrowing, Consolidated Fund, expenditure charged on Consolidated Fund, appropriation, etc.

q:
With reference to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
1. Advocate General is under Art 165.
2. UPSC is under Art 315.
3. CAG holds office for 6 years or 65 years of age, whichever earlier (as provided).
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Correct statements: 1, 2, 3. Incorrect: none. This follows the standard UPSC three-statement option codes.

q:
With reference to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
1. Attorney General is under Art 76.
2. Attorney General has right of audience in all Indian courts.
3. UPSC is concerned with All-India and Central Services recruitment advice.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Correct statements: 1, 2, 3. Incorrect: none. This follows the standard UPSC three-statement option codes.

q: The National Development Council (NDC) is chaired by:
explain: The National Development Council is chaired by the Prime Minister. It includes all Union Cabinet Ministers, Chief Ministers of all States, Lt. Governors/Administrators of UTs, and members of NITI Aayog.

q: The Preamble is considered to be:
opts: A part of the Constitution (Supreme Court's Kesavananda Bharati Case, 1973)
Not a part of the Constitution
explain: Initially in Berubari Union Case (1960), the SC said Preamble is not part of the Constitution. But in Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973), the SC held that the Preamble IS a part of the Constitution and can be amended (but not the basic structure).

q: Which writ prevents a lower court from proceeding in a matter outside its jurisdiction?
explain: Prohibition prevents a lower court/tribunal from exercising jurisdiction it does not have or from exceeding its jurisdiction. Certiorari quashes an order already passed; Prohibition prevents the order from being passed.

q: Which article of the Constitution deals with the Right to Freedom of Religion?
explain: Articles 25-28 deal with the Right to Freedom of Religion: freedom of conscience, freedom to manage religious affairs, freedom from religious taxes, and religious instruction in educational institutions.

q: 'Letter Jurisdiction' of High Courts is under:
explain: Article 226 gives High Courts power to issue writs (Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Certiorari, Prohibition, Quo Warranto) for enforcement of Fundamental Rights and other legal rights.

q: Freedom of press in India is derived from which Article?
explain: Freedom of the press is implicitly included in Article 19(1)(a) — Freedom of speech and expression. The Supreme Court has held press freedom is a part of this fundamental right.

q: What is the supreme law of India?
explain: The Constitution of India is the supreme law of the land. All other laws must be consistent with it.

q: The Governor's rule in a state (Article 356) was first imposed in:
explain: Article 356 (President's Rule) was first imposed in Punjab in 1951. It has been imposed over 100 times since independence — Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh have had it most often.

q: Article 356 (President's Rule) was interpreted in which landmark case to require 'objective satisfaction'?
opts: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)
explain: In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court held that imposition of President's Rule is subject to judicial review and the President must have 'objective satisfaction' based on relevant material.

q: The Indian Constitution came into force on:
explain: The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950 (Republic Day).

q:
With reference to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
1. NITI Aayog is a constitutional body.
2. National Commission for Backward Classes has constitutional status under Art 338B.
3. Comptroller functions of CAG include propriety audit aspects in practice.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Correct statements: 2, 3. Incorrect: 1. This follows the standard UPSC three-statement option codes.

q: Part II of the Constitution (Articles 5-11) deals with:
explain: Part II (Articles 5-11) deals with Citizenship — at the commencement of the Constitution. The details of citizenship are governed by the Citizenship Act 1955.

q: The Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha is elected by:
explain: The Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha is elected by the members of Lok Sabha from among themselves (Article 93). Similarly, the Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha is elected by its members.

q:
With reference to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
1. Attorney General is under Art 76.
2. Advocate General is under Art 165.
3. National Commission for Backward Classes has constitutional status under Art 338B.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Correct statements: 1, 2, 3. Incorrect: none. This follows the standard UPSC three-statement option codes.

q: The 74th Constitutional Amendment relates to:
explain: The 74th Amendment (1992) constitutionalized Urban Local Bodies — Nagar Panchayats, Municipal Councils, Municipal Corporations. It added Part IX-A (Arts 243P-243ZG) and the 12th Schedule.

q: Which article of the Constitution prohibits child labour (below 14 years) in factories and hazardous employment?
explain: Article 24 prohibits employment of children below 14 years in factories, mines, or other hazardous employment.

q: The Chairman of NITI Aayog is:
explain: The Prime Minister is the ex-officio Chairman of NITI Aayog. It also has a CEO (appointed by PM), Vice Chairman, and Governing Council (all CMs and LGs of states/UTs).

q: Which case established that the President must act on the advice of the Council of Ministers?
opts: Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974)
explain: Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974) — the Supreme Court held that the President and Governors are constitutional heads and must act on the advice of the Cabinet/Council of Ministers.

q: A Constitutional Amendment Bill rejected by Rajya Sabha:
opts: Cannot be passed through joint sitting
explain: Constitutional Amendment Bills CANNOT be passed through a joint sitting of Parliament (unlike ordinary bills which can). Rajya Sabha's rejection of a Constitutional Amendment Bill means it fails.

q: Which Article deals with the official language of the Union?
explain: Article 343 states Hindi in Devanagari script shall be the official language of the Union. English was also continued as an official language by the Official Languages Act, 1963.

q: Which Fundamental Right is available to both citizens and non-citizens?
explain: Article 14 (Equality before law) applies to 'any person' — both citizens and non-citizens. Similarly, Articles 20, 21, 21A, 22, 25-28 apply to all persons, not just citizens.

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. CAG audits Union and State accounts.
2. Attorney General is under Art 76.
3. Advocate General is under Art 165.
4. NITI Aayog is a constitutional body.
How many of the above statements are correct?
explain: Exactly 3 of the four statements are constitutionally correct; hence 'Only three'.

q:
With reference to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
1. NITI Aayog is a constitutional body.
2. NCST is under Art 338A.
3. Attorney General has right of audience in all Indian courts.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Correct statements: 2, 3. Incorrect: 1. This follows the standard UPSC three-statement option codes.

q: Who is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha?
explain: The Vice President of India is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

q: The 'First Past The Post' (FPTP) electoral system used in Lok Sabha elections means:
opts: Candidate with most votes wins, even without majority
Second round run-off if no majority
explain: In FPTP, the candidate who gets the most votes (plurality) in a constituency wins, even if they do not have an absolute majority.

q: What is the minimum age for a person to become a member of Rajya Sabha?
explain: A person must be at least 30 years old to be elected to the Rajya Sabha.

q: The official language of the Union of India is:
explain: Article 343: Hindi in Devanagari script is the official language of the Union. English continues to be used for official purposes under Article 343(2). India has no 'national language'.

id: polity-263-The first case of PIL in
q: The first case of PIL in India was filed by:
opts: Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979)
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987)
explain: Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979) is considered the first PIL in India, filed by advocate Kapila Hingorani for undertrial prisoners. Justice P.N. Bhagwati was instrumental in developing PIL jurisprudence.

q:
With reference to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
1. NITI Aayog is a constitutional body.
2. NCST is under Art 338A.
3. UPSC is concerned with All-India and Central Services recruitment advice.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Correct statements: 2, 3. Incorrect: 1. This follows the standard UPSC three-statement option codes.

q: The Rajya Sabha has special powers to resolve that Parliament can legislate on State subjects under:
explain: Art 249: Rajya Sabha by 2/3rd majority can declare it necessary for Parliament to legislate on a State subject in national interest. Art 250: During National Emergency, Parliament can legislate on State List.

id: polity-2-On which date did the In
q: On which date did the Indian Constitution come into force?
explain: The Indian Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, celebrated as Republic Day.

q: The term 'prorogation' of Parliament means:
opts: Termination of a session without dissolution
explain: Prorogation terminates a session of Parliament. Bills pending at prorogation lapse (except those before joint committees or passed by one House). Adjournment only terminates a sitting for a shorter period.

id: polity-35-How is the Speaker of Lo
q: How is the Speaker of Lok Sabha elected?
opts: Elected by all Lok Sabha members
explain: The Speaker of Lok Sabha is elected from among the members of the Lok Sabha by its members.

q: What does 'Republic' mean in Indian context (as in 'Sovereign Democratic Republic')?
opts: The head of state is elected, not hereditary
India has no head of state
India's PM is elected by people
explain: Republic means the head of state (President) is elected by the people's representatives, not hereditary like a monarch.

q: Which schedule lists the official languages of India?
explain: 8th Schedule originally listed 14 official languages. Currently it has 22 languages. Tamil was one of the original 14 languages.

q: The maximum size of the Council of Ministers cannot exceed:
explain: 91st Constitutional Amendment (2003): Council of Ministers strength shall not exceed 15% of total membership of the Lower House (Lok Sabha). Similarly for state cabinets.

id: polity-60-The Rajya Sabha is a per
q: The Rajya Sabha is a permanent body because:
opts: It is never dissolved — only 1/3 of its members retire every 2 years
It has more powers than Lok Sabha
Its members are elected for 10 years
explain: Rajya Sabha is a permanent body (Article 83) — it is never dissolved. Each member serves a 6-year term, and 1/3 of its members retire every 2 years. Currently has 245 members (238 elected + 12 nominated by President for expertise in arts, science, literature, social service).

q: The 'Joint Sitting' of both Houses of Parliament is presided over by:
explain: A joint sitting of Parliament (under Article 108) is presided over by the Speaker of Lok Sabha.

q: The State Election Commission (for local body elections) was established by:
explain: The 73rd and 74th Amendments made it mandatory for states to establish State Election Commissions (Article 243K for Panchayats, 243ZA for Municipalities) to superintend, direct, and control elections to local bodies.

q: The 74th Constitutional Amendment Act (1992) related to:
explain: 74th Amendment (1992) added Part IXA and the 12th Schedule, giving constitutional status to urban local bodies (Municipal Corporations, Municipal Councils, Nagar Panchayats). 12th Schedule lists 18 functions for municipalities.

q: Which case upheld the power of Parliament to amend Fundamental Rights (later overruled)?
explain: Sankari Prasad case (1951) and Sajjan Singh case (1965): SC held Parliament has power to amend any provision of the Constitution including Fundamental Rights. This was overruled in Golaknath (1967).

q: Who can summon and prorogue sessions of Parliament?
opts: President on the advice of Cabinet
explain: The President summons each House of Parliament (Art 85), prorogues the Houses, and dissolves the Lok Sabha — always on the advice of the Council of Ministers (Cabinet).

q: Under which Article can the Supreme Court review its own judgments?
explain: Article 137 empowers the Supreme Court to review any judgment pronounced or order made by it, subject to any law made by Parliament or rules made under Art 145. Review petitions must be filed within 30 days.

q: Which schedule of the Constitution deals with anti-defection law?
explain: The Tenth Schedule (added by the 52nd Amendment, 1985) contains provisions for disqualification on grounds of defection.

q:
Consider the following matching exercise.
Which is a correct application of Article 51?
opts: Guiding India's approach to international peace, just international order, and respect for international law
Creating a Fundamental Right to asylum enforceable by writ always
Replacing the UN Charter in Indian law automatically
explain: Article 51 is a foreign-policy oriented DPSP.

q: The President's 'Pocket Veto' refers to:
opts: Returning a bill for reconsideration indefinitely without acting
Sending to Supreme Court for opinion
explain: Pocket Veto is an informal term for the President's power to keep a bill pending without returning it — effectively killing it. This has been used once by President Zail Singh (1986, Postal Amendment Bill).

q:
With reference to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
1. Advocate General is under Art 165.
2. UPSC is under Art 315.
3. NHRC is a constitutional body under Art 338B.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Correct statements: 1, 2. Incorrect: 3. This follows the standard UPSC three-statement option codes.

id: polity-71-A judge of the Supreme C
q: A judge of the Supreme Court can be removed by:
opts: President on the recommendation of PM
Parliament's impeachment (special majority in both Houses)
explain: A Supreme Court judge can only be removed by the President on an address of Parliament — both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha must pass the resolution by a special majority (majority of total membership + 2/3 of members present and voting). This is called impeachment.

q:
With reference to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
1. Attorney General is under Art 76.
2. Advocate General is under Art 165.
3. UPSC is under Art 315.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Correct statements: 1, 2, 3. Incorrect: none. This follows the standard UPSC three-statement option codes.

id: polity-186-A Money Bill can be intr
q: A Money Bill can be introduced in:
explain: A Money Bill (as defined under Art 110) can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha on the recommendation of the President. Rajya Sabha can only recommend amendments — Lok Sabha may or may not accept.

q: A Starred Question in Parliament is:
opts: An oral answer question with supplementaries
explain: A Starred Question (marked with *) requires an oral answer in the House and allows supplementary questions by the member. About 20 starred questions are listed per sitting day.

q: Under which Article can Parliament restrict fundamental rights during a National Emergency?
explain: Art 358 suspends Art 19 during external emergency automatically. Art 359 allows President to suspend enforcement of other FRs (except Arts 20 & 21) by order during any emergency.

q: What is the quorum required to conduct business in the Lok Sabha?
explain: The quorum to constitute a meeting of either House of Parliament is one-tenth of the total number of members of the House (Art 100). For Lok Sabha (543 members), this means at least 55 members.

q: The Estimates Committee of Parliament has how many members?
explain: The Estimates Committee has 30 members, all from Lok Sabha. It examines the estimates in the budget and suggests economies in expenditure. Rajya Sabha has no representation.

q: 'Curative Petition' in the Supreme Court was recognized in which case?
opts: Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002)
explain: The concept of a Curative Petition was established in Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002). It is the last constitutional remedy after the SC dismisses a review petition.

q: Can High Courts issue all 5 writs?
opts: Yes, under Article 226 (and for FRs under Article 226)
No, only SC can issue all 5
HC can issue only Habeas Corpus
HC can issue writs only for FRs
explain: Article 226 gives High Courts power to issue all 5 writs — not just for enforcement of Fundamental Rights but also for 'any other purpose'. SC under Article 32 issues writs only for FR enforcement.

q: Identify the correct Article for the theme: Finance Commission
explain: Finance Commission is under Article 280.

q: The writ 'Mandamus' is issued to:
opts: Lower courts to stop exceeding jurisdiction
A public official or body to perform a legal duty they have neglected or refused to perform
A person to justify why they hold a public office
Produce a detained person before court
explain: Mandamus ('we command') is a writ directing a public official, lower court, government body, or corporation to perform a mandatory public duty that it has failed or refused to perform. Cannot be issued against a private person.

q: Which Article is correctly matched with 'Salaries of Supreme Court judges'?
explain: Salaries of Supreme Court judges is under Article 125.

q: The Chief Election Commissioner of India can be removed by:
opts: Same process as a Supreme Court judge
explain: The Chief Election Commissioner can be removed only through the same process as a Supreme Court judge — by an address of both Houses of Parliament passed by special majority (Article 324).

q: Article 14 of the Indian Constitution guarantees:
opts: Right to Equality before law and Equal protection of laws
Right to Life and Personal Liberty
explain: Article 14: 'The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.' It is available to citizens AND non-citizens.

q:
With reference to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:
1. NITI Aayog is a constitutional body.
2. UPSC is under Art 315.
3. UPSC is concerned with All-India and Central Services recruitment advice.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
explain: Correct statements: 2, 3. Incorrect: 1. This follows the standard UPSC three-statement option codes.

q: The 7th Schedule divides subjects into:
explain: 7th Schedule: (1) Union List (100 subjects) — Parliament only, (2) State List (61 subjects) — State Legislature, (3) Concurrent List (52 subjects) — Both; Parliament prevails in case of conflict.

q: India's Constitution is the world's longest written constitution with originally how many articles?
explain: Originally the Constitution had 395 articles in 22 parts and 8 schedules. Currently it has 448 articles (as amended) in 25 parts and 12 schedules (as of 2023).

q: The procedure for amending the Constitution is in:
explain: Article 368 deals with the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution. There are three methods: simple majority (certain provisions), special majority (2/3 of members present and voting + majority of total membership), and special majority + ratification by half the state legislatures.

q: Which DPSP article relates to promotion of cottage industries in rural areas?
explain: Article 43 directs the State to secure to all workers a living wage, decent standard of life and to promote cottage industries on individual or cooperative basis in rural areas.

q: The concept of 'Constitutional Morality' was highlighted in which recent Supreme Court case?
opts: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018)
Joseph Shine v. Union of India (2018)
explain: Both Navtej Singh Johar (decriminalising Section 377) and Joseph Shine (striking down adultery law) relied heavily on Constitutional Morality — adherence to constitutional values, not social morality.

q: The three-tier Panchayati Raj structure recommended by the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee consists of:
opts: Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti, Zila Parishad
Gram Panchayat, Block Panchayat, District Board
Village Council, Taluk Board, District Council
Gram Sabha, Gram Panchayat, District Panchayat
explain: The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended a 3-tier structure: Gram Panchayat (village level), Panchayat Samiti (block level), and Zila Parishad (district level). This was formally adopted by the 73rd Amendment as the model.

q: The Preamble to the Indian Constitution was amended by which amendment?
explain: The 42nd Amendment (1976) added three words to the Preamble: 'Socialist', 'Secular', and 'Integrity'.

q: Inter-State River Water Disputes are adjudicated by:
opts: Tribunals under Article 262 and Inter-State Water Disputes Act
explain: Article 262 empowers Parliament to provide for adjudication of disputes relating to use, distribution, or control of inter-state rivers. Parliament enacted the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act 1956.

q:
Assertion (A): India has a federal system with a unitary bias.
Reason (R): During an Emergency, the Centre can assume greater control over the states.
Select the correct answer using the codes below.
opts: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
Assertion is true but Reason is false
Assertion is false but Reason is true
explain: Both true; emergency centralisation is a classic unitary feature explaining the bias.

q: Which Union Territory has its own Legislature and High Court?
explain: Delhi (National Capital Territory) and Puducherry are the only UTs with their own Legislative Assemblies (and thus elected governments). J&K is now a UT with Legislature after 2019.

q: With reference to the Constitution of India, protection against double jeopardy is provided under:
explain: Article 20(2) provides that no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once.

q: The principle 'One Vote, One Value' in Indian elections means:
opts: Each vote has equal value — no plural voting
Only one person can vote per family
explain: The principle of 'One Person, One Vote, One Value' ensures universal adult franchise — each citizen above 18 years has one vote of equal value, regardless of wealth, gender, religion, or caste.

q: The 44th Amendment Act (1978) restricted the use of National Emergency by:
opts: Requiring Cabinet's written recommendation and 2/3 majority approval
explain: The 44th Amendment (1978, post-Emergency) changed 'internal disturbance' to 'armed rebellion' (harder standard), required Cabinet's written recommendation, required approval by special majority (2/3 of total membership), and gave Lok Sabha power to revoke Emergency by simple majority.

q: The minimum number of members required to sign a notice of No-Confidence Motion is:
explain: A No-Confidence Motion can be introduced in Lok Sabha if at least 50 members support it (notice signed by minimum 50 members). The Speaker then admits the motion.

q: With reference to the Constitution of India, who decides whether a Bill is a Money Bill?
explain: Speaker's decision on Money Bill is final.

q: Under which article can the President proclaim a National Emergency?
explain: Article 352 empowers the President to proclaim a National Emergency if the security of India is threatened by war, external aggression, or armed rebellion.

q: The Speaker of Lok Sabha is elected by:
explain: The Speaker of Lok Sabha is elected by the members of Lok Sabha from among themselves (Art 93). The Speaker can be removed by a resolution of the House by a majority of all the then members.

q:
With reference to the Constitution of India, consider the following statements:

q: Which Article defines 'State' for the purpose of Fundamental Rights?

q: With reference to the Constitution of India, separation of judiciary from executive is directed by:

q: Article 32 (Right to move Supreme Court) is itself a:
explain: Article 32 — the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights — is itself a Fundamental Right under Part III. It cannot be suspended except during National Emergency (Art 359 order by President).

q: Article 143 empowers the President to seek advisory opinion from:
explain: Article 143: The President can refer any question of law or fact of public importance to the Supreme Court for its advisory opinion. The SC may give or refuse to give the opinion.

q: The 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002) relates to:

explain: 86th Amendment (2002): Added Article 21A (Free and Compulsory Education for 6-14 years as Fundamental Right), amended Article 45 DPSP, and added 11th Fundamental Duty.

q: The Advocate General of a State is appointed by:

q: The Indian Constitution was adopted on:
explain: The Indian Constitution was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949 (Constitution Day/Samvidhan Divas). It came into force on 26 January 1950 (Republic Day). The Constituent Assembly took 2 years, 11 months, 18 days.

q: A money bill is defined in:

q: Under Article 163, the Governor can act in his discretion regarding:

q: Article 368 deals with:
explain: Article 368 (Part XX) provides for the amendment of the Constitution. Parliament can amend any provision of the Constitution (subject to the Basic Structure doctrine established in Kesavananda Bharati case).

q: 73rd Constitutional Amendment relates to:
explain: 73rd Amendment gave constitutional status to PRIs.

q: The Anti-Defection Law is contained in which Schedule?
explain: The Anti-Defection Law is in the 10th Schedule, added by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment (1985). It disqualifies members of Parliament and State Legislatures for defecting from their party.

q: The Vice-President of India is elected by:
opts: Members of Electoral College (same as President)
Members of both Houses of Parliament (Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha) — not state legislatures
explain: The Vice-President is elected by members of both Houses of Parliament (Article 66) — Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. State legislators are NOT part of this electoral process (unlike President's election).

q: Financial Emergency (Article 360) has been invoked in India:
explain: Financial Emergency under Article 360 has NEVER been proclaimed in India since independence. It can be proclaimed when the financial stability or credit of India or any state is threatened.

q: Under which article can Parliament legislate on State List subjects?
explain: Parliament can legislate on State List under: Art. 249 (RS resolution for national interest), Art. 250 (during Emergency), Art. 252 (2 or more states request), Art. 253 (for treaty/agreement).

q: E.P. Royappa (1974) is best associated with:

q: Rajya Sabha's special power to authorize Parliament to legislate on State subjects is under:
explain: Article 249: If Rajya Sabha passes a resolution by 2/3rd majority that it is necessary in national interest, Parliament can legislate on a State List subject for 1 year (renewable).

q: Contingency Fund of India is established under:
explain: Article 267: Contingency Fund of India enables the President to make advances to meet unforeseen expenditure (limit ₹500 crore). Parliament approval is later sought to recoup the amount.

q: Which article of the Indian Constitution deals with the formation of new States?
explain: Article 3 empowers Parliament to admit new States, form new States from existing ones, alter boundaries or change names.

q: Which article of the Constitution talks about abolition of titles?
explain: Article 18 abolishes titles: No title shall be conferred by the State. Citizens cannot accept titles from foreign governments without President's consent. Exceptions: Military/academic distinctions.

q: President's Rule (Article 356) in a state lasts initially for:
explain: President's Rule (State Emergency) lasts initially for 6 months, can be extended for a maximum of 3 years (with Parliamentary approval every 6 months after first 6 months).

q: The maximum strength of a State Legislative Assembly is:
explain: Article 170: State Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha) can have not more than 500 members and not less than 60 members (except Goa, Sikkim, Mizoram, Nagaland have less than 60).

q: Parliamentary Sovereignty in India means:
opts: Parliament has supreme power within Constitutional limits
explain: Unlike UK's absolute Parliamentary sovereignty, India has limited parliamentary sovereignty — Parliament is supreme within constitutional limits. Courts can strike down laws violating the Constitution.

q: Articles 23 and 24 deal with:
explain: Articles 23-24 (Right against Exploitation): Art. 23 prohibits human trafficking and forced labor (begar). Art. 24 prohibits employment of children below 14 years in factories/mines/hazardous work.

q: The 101st Constitutional Amendment (2016) introduced:
explain: 101st Constitutional Amendment (September 2016) introduced the Goods and Services Tax (GST) — a comprehensive indirect tax replacing multiple central and state taxes.

q: The 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) changed the term 'internal disturbance' in Art 352 to:

q: The minimum age for voting in India is:

q: Protection against self-incrimination is guaranteed by:

q: The two-party system in Tamil Nadu politics refers to:

q: The Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973) established the doctrine of:

q: Article 17 abolishes:

q: Under which Articles are protection against arbitrary arrest and detention provided?

q: The 44th Amendment Act (1978) is significant because:

q: Tamil Nadu State Legislature is:

explain: Article 32 gives the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Dr. Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.
